## You said: How much water does turkey use?

How much water does turkey use? Like the food not the country

## Claude responded: Turkey usually gets lumped in with poultry, and the commonly cited figure is around 4,300 litres per kilogram, the :antCitation\[\]{citations="8f36af01-4dce-4d51…

Searched the web

Searched the web

Turkey usually gets lumped in with poultry, and the commonly cited figure is around 4,300 litres per kilogram, the [The Poultry Site](https://www.thepoultrysite.com/news/2016/04/how-much-water-does-it-take-to-produce-meat) same ballpark as chicken — roughly 520 gallons per pound, [Spokesman-Review](https://www.spokesman.com/stories/2021/feb/17/zoe-south-the-water-footprint-of-red-meat/) which works out to about the same. Some sources put it lower, around 2,400 litres per kilogram. [CWR](https://cwrrr.org/opinions/stuff-the-turkey/) A lot of the British/Christmas estimates you'll see actually just use chicken figures as a stand-in for turkey, [World Economic Forum](https://www.weforum.org/stories/2016/12/how-much-water-do-you-need-to-make-your-favourite-christmas-meals/) since turkey is rarely measured separately.

The spread between sources (2,400 vs 4,300) is the part worth caring about, and it comes down to method. The big caveat is the green/blue/grey split: the overwhelming majority of that number is **green water** — rain that falls on the feed crops and would've fallen anyway. Across the meat sector, about 98 percent of the footprint goes to producing animal feed, [FoodPrint](https://foodprint.org/issues/the-water-footprint-of-food/) and only 10–20 percent of the headline figure is water that's actually consumed rather than returned to the natural cycle. [The Poultry Site](https://www.thepoultrysite.com/news/2016/04/how-much-water-does-it-take-to-produce-meat) The **blue water** (irrigation drawn from rivers/aquifers — the part that genuinely competes with other uses) is a small slice.

So if you want the honest version: ~4,000 L/kg as a green-inclusive footprint, but the freshwater-you'd-actually-trade-off number is far smaller and depends heavily on whether the birds' feed was rainfed or irrigated.

For your water-comparison site this is a useful one to flag, since the "X litres per burger/turkey" stats almost always quote the green-inclusive number against AI figures that are mostly blue water — not an apples-to-apples comparison.

Jun 21

## Claude responded: Short version: there's no datable "sudden loss of cheap potable water" event on the horizon — not for the US, not for your stretch of the Front Range.

Searched the web

Searched the web

Short version: there's no datable "sudden loss of cheap potable water" event on the horizon — not for the US, not for your stretch of the Front Range. The honest model is gradual erosion of the _cheap_ part, studded with sudden, local _availability_ shocks that fire when a specific buffer fails. And the Iran sequence is a surprisingly good calibration device for exactly why that's the right answer and not a dodge — because it ran the experiment twice and got opposite-looking results that combine into one coherent lesson.

**What the two Iran episodes actually taught.** In June 2025, first-order theory said: US strikes Iran → Iran closes Hormuz → oil shock. The trade was obvious and everyone had it on. Then Iran simply didn't close the strait, despite reportedly prepping to mine it, [Congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R45281) oil spiked intraday and sold off, and the market shrugged — because closing it was against Iran's own interest, so the predicted discontinuity kept _not happening_. Classic case of buffering and rational self-interest cancelling a catastrophe that theory treated as mechanical.

Then in early 2026 the tail actually fired. After a decapitation strike that killed Khamenei, Iran declared the strait closed and began mining it, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Strait_of_Hormuz_crisis) and you got the real thing: a historic oil shock, gas at the highest since 2022, Brent jawboned back toward $119 on a Trump deadline, then an 11% drop the moment de-escalation was signaled. [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2026/04/business/timeline-strait-of-hormuz-global-economy/) Note the shape — not a smooth ramp into a wall, but a violent punctuation, gapping up on headlines and back down on de-escalation, and ultimately a _transient_: painful spike, then reconvergence as substitution (domestic supply, the never-used SPR option) and the fact that sustaining it served nobody pulled it back.

Combine them and the lesson isn't "markets shrug" or "catastrophe" — it's: **adaptive systems keep cancelling the predicted shock right up until a buffer breaks, and the long run of cancelled predictions is precisely what makes the eventual punctuation feel like it came from nowhere.** The thing that smooths the system in normal times (everyone avoiding the mutually destructive equilibrium) is the same thing that hides how much slack has been drawn down.

**Now map that onto water, with the Colorado River as the worked example** — which matters to you directly, since the Front Range pulls transmountain Colorado River water on top of the South Platte. The "normal regime" is heavily engineered buffering: tiered shortage declarations (Tier Zero in 2021, Tier One in 2022/24/25, Tier Two in 2023), paid conservation, and emergency transfers from upstream reservoirs like Flaming Gorge. [Congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R45546) Every year somebody predicts Day Zero and every year it gets negotiated down one tier — the strait-stays-open dynamic. That trains everyone to assume perpetual muddle-through.

Underneath, the slack is visibly shrinking. Lake Mead is down roughly 160 feet since 2000, [Southern Nevada Water Authority](https://www.snwa.com/water-resources/drought-and-shortage/index.html) and Powell is forecast to flirt with minimum power pool (3,490 ft) by August 2026 on one of the lowest inflows on record — about 29% of average. [Bureau of Reclamation](https://www.usbr.gov/newsroom/news-release/5326) And there's a genuine governance cliff dated to the end of next year: the 2007 shortage guidelines, the 2019 drought plans, and parts of the Mexico treaty all expire at the end of 2026, the seven states still don't agree, and the feds have started moving ahead with their own 10-year plan. [Briefs Finance](https://www.briefs.co/news/colorado-river-rules-expire-end-of-2026/) That's a _legal/political_ discontinuity, not a tap-runs-dry one — but it's the analogue of the decapitation strike: the event that can remove the buffering machinery itself.

So "sudden or gradual" resolves like this: the **cheap** degrades permanently and gradually — buy-and-dry of ag water rights, rising tap fees, xeriscaping mandates, ag-to-urban reallocation — over one to three decades. The **available** degrades suddenly but locally and mostly transiently, when a drought year lands on already-depleted storage and a specific buffer (a reservoir hitting dead/power pool, a failed allocation deal, a contamination event) gives way. Cape Town's 2018 Day Zero is the canonical shape: gradual for years, then "weeks away," then defused by emergency rationing and pricing. Sharp, painful, not civilizational, and it reconverged at a higher cost basis — exactly like the oil spike.

For you specifically on the Front Range: you're upper-basin and municipally well-buffered, so your realistic exposure isn't the tap going dry — it's the price of "cheap" climbing steadily, plus a non-zero chance of a hard drought-year curtailment if storage and the post-2026 framework both go badly at once. The datable thing to watch is the end-2026 framework expiry and whatever the feds impose; the undatable thing is the multi-decade ramp that's already running. The trap, per the Iran lesson, is reading a decade of successfully-negotiated tiers as evidence it'll always be negotiable — that's the calm before someone closes the strait.

Jun 21
